🐾 Found it! Matt’s payments work at **JP Morgan Chase** centered on building ACCESS Next Generation, from **August 2009** through **June 2012**.

The bank was consolidating regional treasury and cash-management systems into a single global portal. Bottomline Technologies’ WebSeries platform provided the foundation, but its out-of-box capabilities did not cover the payment workflows, security controls, and regulatory requirements of **135,000+ clients** across **180+ countries**. Regional systems also had different data models, entitlement structures, and transaction histories that had to move without interrupting live payments.

As Technology Delivery Lead, Matt managed a blended team of **40+** **Accenture** and bank resources across the US, Mumbai, and Bangalore. He spent **70 to 80%** of his time embedded at Bottomline’s Portsmouth offices, determining where platform configuration ended and bespoke engineering was required.

He designed and delivered ACH, wire, FX/cross-border, and tax-payment modules, including NACHA file validation, embedded FX rate visibility, and Message Authentication Code security for payment verification before release. He also built the centralized payments gateway, handling message transformation, protocol translation, and routing across **12 countries**, replacing fragmented point-to-point integrations.

For corporate administrators, Matt introduced bulk permission changes across users, accounts, and products from a single screen. Payment-type-specific controls could authorize someone to approve wires without allowing FX initiation. Entitlement management dropped from days to minutes.

Matt also led payments data migration without disruption to live payment operations. For the global rollout, he translated regional regulatory requirements into data-visibility and access-control configurations, sequencing launches by regulatory readiness rather than using a single big-bang deployment.

ACCESS launched in **April 2011**. Corporate treasurers gained a single entry point for payments across regions, with real-time global reporting and access to cash, trade, and investment operations through the same portal.

🐾 Matt leads with empathy, clarity, and purpose.

He describes teams he inherited as “over-processed, under-trusted, waiting for permission instead of owning outcomes.” His focus is on removing those barriers: making intent explicit, creating psychological safety so people speak honestly, and pushing decisions to the people closest to the work. He coaches teams to think clearly, not just execute tasks.

At the **Accenture** Cloud Innovation Center, that included a “permit to fail” learning environment. Teams had avoided risks because they feared blame. Matt organized non-punitive post-mortems, emphasized lessons rather than pointing fingers, and supported lean, low-stakes experiments. In innovation engagements, he set expectations upfront that prototypes and user tests would likely fail. Teams used those results to challenge assumptions and shape product direction week by week, before committing to costly builds.

He also brought engineers, product managers, and UX architects into balanced teams with equal participation and shared accountability. Rather than relying on handoffs between separate functions, he embedded pair programming, collaborative coding, stand-ups, retrospectives, and knowledge-sharing sessions. Teams connected their goals to client and business outcomes and could voice feedback and change their workflows autonomously.

His working principles include integrity and respect, continuous learning, and “outcomes, not optics.” Engineering practices remain part of that philosophy: automation, continuous delivery, and quality-first practices. At the Cloud Innovation Center, teams achieved **4x delivery acceleration** after embracing lean product and modern engineering practices. The balanced-team work also achieved **zero-defect production code** through iterative development and real-time feedback loops.

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s what Matt has built and delivered.

Matt’s work spans execution and delivery, organizational transformation, and talent development: enterprise platforms shipped across **12 countries**, troubled programs recovered, and an engineering organization built from **0 to 150+ practitioners**.

At **Accenture**, clients needed more than another software delivery program. They were working through slow development cycles, fragmented workflows, legacy systems, and handoffs between product, design, and engineering. Many new hires also lacked hands-on experience with cloud-native technologies or modern engineering practices.

Matt built the Atlanta and Tampa Cloud Innovation Centers with full P&L accountability. Instead of keeping product managers, designers, and engineers in separate functions, he established balanced teams. Instead of a separate QA phase, teams used test-driven development and automated pipelines. Instead of delivering a large requirements list before getting feedback, they shipped thin-slice, production-ready solutions and used customer feedback to decide what came next.

He built training around “I do, we do, you do,” pairing junior practitioners with experienced mentors and using coding katas, workshops, and hands-on delivery. The talent program achieved near-zero attrition in its first **2 years**.

When delivery fell short, he addressed the work directly. At **Norfolk Southern**, rising defects contradicted near-complete test coverage. Matt took ownership, audited the code and tests, exposed vague backlog stories, and brought in TDD experts to work alongside the team. The client stopped finding defects the dashboard could not see. At **JP Morgan Chase**, CIC teams outpaced peer velocity within the first **2 sprints**.

The centers delivered **30+ product engagements** across **15+ clients**, with **4X faster velocity** and **zero-defect deployments**. Matt drove **\$100M+ in repeat business** through delivery excellence and customer relationships. Clients kept coming back, and teams continued using the practices after engagements ended.

question: Why hire Matt?

answer_md:
🐾 Here’s a time Matt’s assumptions led to a real incident.

Matt was the tech lead on a global platform modernization for a financial services client. The program was under delivery pressure, with offshore teams running test cycles across development, QA, UAT, and production. IAM controls, environment segregation, and downstream access configurations had been inherited from earlier phases.

Matt was responsible for ensuring a safe environment setup. He relied on the inherited documentation instead of verifying the IAM configuration and downstream access controls. He did not audit who could trigger email processes, confirm that production customer data had been scrubbed from test environments, or implement compensating controls such as data masking and email interception.

An offshore tester accidentally triggered an email job in UAT. It sent communications containing unmasked production customer data to **thousands of real clients**.

Matt took accountability and led the team through root cause analysis and remediation. They identified insufficient IAM checks, unclear environment boundaries, and production data that had not been scrubbed from downstream environments. He worked with the team to understand what happened and implement corrective controls.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” After the incident, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach.

The client nevertheless demanded that the tester be removed from the project. Matt described that as “a systemic failure that resulted in an individual consequence.”

His stated lesson was that “assumptions are risks in disguise.” After the incident, he made IAM validation, environment verification, PII scrubbing, and risk ownership day-one responsibilities in his delivery approach.
